newsitem.title: GERMANY: FORECAST-Mark to recover against dollar before EMU.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Mark to recover against dollar before EMU.

text.p: The mark, languishing due to the weak German economy, should hit bottom in mid-1997 before steadily recovering against the dollar ahead of the planned 1999 start of the euro, a Reuter survey showed on Wednesday.
The disparity between the healthy U.S. economy and Germany, hampered by record joblessness, should keep the mark under pressure at least through the 1997 second quarter, the survey showed.

The survey of 30 European financial institutions, which was completed between January 13-15 and so before the U.S. currency's recent growth spurt -- showed a mean forecast of 1.577 marks for the dollar at the end of the first quarter.
Sterling was pegged at 2.6174 marks at the end of March and at 2.6263 marks at the end of the second quarter. The yen was expected to end the first quarter at 73.12 marks.
Both sterling and the yen should then generally weaken against the mark over the next seven quarters through the 1998 fourth quarter, according to the survey results.
The dollar should peak in the 1997 second quarter at 1.5888 marks before steadily sliding through the balance of 1997 and early 1998 until reaching 1.5579 marks in the 1998 fourth quarter.
The dollar has staged a dramatic rally since the survey was conducted, rising five pfennigs from the January 13 level of 1.58 marks to its recent peak at 1.6315 marks on January 21.
Some economists said the dollar would see its glory fade in the coming months.
They saw it slipping to as low as 1.45 marks ahead of the start of the new European currency, shared by a small group of countries led by Germany and France but not Spain, Italy and Portugual.

Matthias Joerss, economist at MM Warburg in Hamburg, said the dollar has so far been carried due to the widening spread between German and U.S. interest rates, prompted by hopes for one or two small U.S. rate hikes in the coming months.
"We are now in the process of pricing a cut or two into the market, but we will still get a reaction in the U.S. stock market, something the Federal Reserve wants," Joerss said.
"If that is the case, then I think we will see a significantly weaker Wall Street and, based on past history, that is bad news for the dollar," he said.

He also said a general view in Europe hoped for a dollar above 1.55 marks to help spur export growth. But he said the U.S. may later seek a weaker dollar to maintain the recovery and trade deficit worries would also likely hamper the currency.

But some economists said the recent dollar gains have only underpinned their outlook -- particularly as the debate about the start of the new European currency slated for January 1999 makes the greenback a safe haven.
"We assume the dollar will generally keep going higher but it is not yet clear whether it will go over 1.70 marks," said Lothar Klausing, senior economist at Dresdner Bank.

He said the German economy was "a bit stronger than people had expected", which will underpin the mark. But the dollar should resume having the upper hand and reach an average 1.65 marks in the 1998 second half.

"The euro is the main argument for the dollar to keep moving higher. We do not know yet under what conditions the euro will come into existence and that will keep the dollar relatively strong," Klausing said.
